A command and control behavior was blocked on host `vnevado-win10r`, which indicated an active infection by malware that could replicate and receive commands from remote attackers. This malware was active, and precautionary measures should be taken to check for residual signs of infection. The process involved had the ID 1332 and ran the command `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`. What is the IP address associated with the Manatee Tempest activity group detected in this security incident?

- DeviceProcessEvents (process/command details)
- DeviceNetworkEvents (network connections)
- AlertEvidence / AlertInfo / SecurityAlert / SecurityIncident (incident-level and threat group info)

I’ll first find the process event, then correlate it to alerts/incidents, and finally look up the Manatee Tempest IP in related threat intel.

Action: execute[
SELECT TOP 50
    Timestamp,

    ProcessId,
    InitiatingProcessId,

FROM DeviceProcessEvents
WHERE DeviceName = 'vnevado-win10r'

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

('2024-06-20 09:44:54.309958+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

This may include deleting all volume shadow copies to impede system restoration. Alongside the usage of `vssblatemp.exe`, another process was used to disable recovery features. What was the command and process ID of the other process involved?

Then, using that table, I can search for other processes on the same host that have command lines indicating disabling recovery features (e.g., `bcdedit`, `wbadmin`, `reagentc`, or other tools) around the same timeframe. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set default recoveryenabled no]', 'vnevado-win10s.vnevado.alpineskihouse.co', '{"MicrosoftDefenderAtp.Category":"Ransomware","MicrosoftDefenderAtp.InvestigationId":null,"MicrosoftDefenderAtp.InvestigationState":"UnsupportedAlertType","LastUpdated":"06/20/2024 09:38:35","IncidentId":"107","DetectionSource":"WindowsDefenderAtp","AssignedTo":"Defender Experts","Determination":null,"Classification":null,"Action":"•	Contact your incident response team. [('e34d562e-ef12-4c4e-9bc0-7c6ae357c015', '2024-06-20 09:19:23.499691+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. Lateral movement to the jump server was conducted using PSExec to IP address `99.83.111.100`.
Potentially compromised assets with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522` exhibited ransomware-like behavior, impacting several devices.
A malicious command and control behavior directed to the URL `http://vectorsandarrows.com/` was blocked.

Thought: I need to locate the alert/incident that mentions a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT), then see which Aad user it’s associated with. The narrative sounds like a security alert: first malware (mimikatz, cmd.exe) then a PRT-access attempt. The AadUserId is likely in an evidence record (AlertEvidence) tied to that alert, possibly in AdditionalFields or AccountObjectId. I’ll:
1) Search SecurityAlert and AlertInfo titles/descriptions for “Primary Refresh Token” or “PRT”.
2) From the matching alert, get its AlertId from AlertInfo/AlertEvidence linkage.
3) Use AlertEvidence.AdditionalFields for that AlertId and extract any AadUserId present.

Action: execute[
SELECT 'SecurityAlert' AS src, AlertName AS title, Description, TimeGenerated
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE AlertName LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR AlertName LIKE '%PRT%'
   OR Description LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR Description LIKE '%PRT%'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'AlertInfo' AS src, Title AS title, NULL AS Description, TimeGenerated
FROM AlertInfo
WHERE Title LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR Title LIKE '%PRT%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated DESC
LIMIT 20;
]

A security incident involving system recovery setting tampering was observed on the device with name `vnevado-win10r`. The incident involved processes `vssblatemp.exe` and `bcdedit.exe` being executed on the host `vnevado-win10r` to potentially disrupt recovery options. Additionally, suspicious hands-on keyboard user behavior was detected around the same time, which might indicate that the user has been compromised. Following these activities, there was an indication of ransomware behavior detected in the file system on a device. Can you determine the AadDeviceId of the host where this ransomware activity was detected?

Thought: We’ve identified the LSASS-related alerts tied to IncidentId 321 and host vnevado-win10v. The question asks about a subsequent alert that mentioned a Windows Sysinternals tool being renamed and executed. That should be another SecurityAlert (likely same IncidentId 321 or close in time) whose text mentions a renamed Sysinternals executable (e.g., procdump, psexec, etc.). I’ll search SecurityAlert for keywords like “Sysinternals”, “renamed”, and common Sysinternals tool names and then read the matching alert’s description/Entities to identify the original tool name.

Action: execute[
SELECT TimeGenerated, DisplayName, AlertName, AlertSeverity, Description, ExtendedProperties, Entities
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE (Description LIKE '%Sysinternals%' OR Description LIKE '%Sysinternal%' 
       OR Description LIKE '%renamed%' 
       OR Description LIKE '%procdump%' OR Description LIKE '%PsExec%' 
       OR Description LIKE '%ProcDump%' OR Description LIKE '%procexp%' 
       OR Description LIKE '%autoruns%' OR Description LIKE '%PsTools%')
   AND ExtendedProperties LIKE '%"IncidentId":"321"%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated;
]

A security incident involving an attempt to access a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected. The PRT is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on various devices, including Windows 10. The incident involved a device with HostName `vnevado-win10s` and AadDeviceId `f5b847aa-8712-4bf6-b4f7-ed6cd89e1505`, where the process `browsercore.exe` (ProcessId `2676` created at `2024-06-20T09:10:59.867384Z`) was running. Attackers may use this to move laterally within the organization. Following this incident, 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on another device during lateral movement. What is the AadDeviceId of this affected device?

Thought: I need to identify where security incidents and malware detections are stored, then link the initial PRT-related incident on host vnevado-win10s with the subsequent lateral-movement malware detection of type 'CommandAndControl'. First, I'll explore the database schema to find relevant tables (e.g., incidents, alerts, devices, malware, lateral movement). Then I will search for entries referencing the given AadDeviceId and process details, and finally find the related incident where malware category 'CommandAndControl' was detected on another device, and extract that device's AadDeviceId.

Action: execute[
SELECT
  TimeGenerated,
  DeviceName,
  FileName,
  FolderPath,
  SHA256,
  ActionType,
  AdditionalFields

  AND (

    AdditionalFields LIKE '%credential%' OR
    AdditionalFields LIKE '%token%' OR
    AdditionalFields LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%' OR
    AdditionalFields LIKE '%PRT%' OR
    AdditionalFields LIKE '%Midnight Blizzard%'

ORDER BY TimeGenerated DESC
LIMIT 200;
]

Thought: From the SecurityAlert entries tied to host vnevado-win11u and the PRT-related activity, we see the “Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)” alert. Its process tree shows:

- WMI spawning PowerShell:
  - CommandLine: powershell -File C:\Scripts\get-userprttoken.ps1
- PowerShell then launches BrowserCore.exe to interact with PRT.

This PowerShell script (get-userprttoken.ps1) is the credential theft tool used to access Primary Refresh Tokens, as described in the Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report and is part of the same multi-stage incident that includes the system recovery tampering (vssblatemp.exe, bcdedit).

Therefore, the malicious credential theft tool executed in this incident is the PowerShell script:

get-userprttoken.ps1

Action: submit[get-userprttoken.ps1]

question_dict.context: A security incident involving the Manatee Tempest activity group was reported. This Russia-based cybercriminal group, which has been active since June 2014, is known for malware campaigns including the Dridex banking trojan. They often gain initial access through methods such as drive-by downloads and malvertising, facilitated by their partnership with Mustard Tempest. SELECT TimeGenerated,
       DeviceName,
       FileName,
       FolderPath,
       ProcessCommandLine,
       InitiatingProcessFileName,
       InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
       ActionType
FROM DeviceProcessEvents
WHERE DeviceName = 'vnevado-win10r'
  AND (
        FileName LIKE '%wmic%' OR
        FileName LIKE '%wmiprvse%' OR
        ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%wmic%' OR
        ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%Win32_Process%' OR
        InitiatingProcessCommandLine LIKE '%wmic%' OR
        InitiatingProcessCommandLine LIKE '%Win32_Process%'
      )
ORDER BY TimeGenerated DESC
LIMIT 50]

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', question_dict.context: A serious security incident involving the Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device. Mimikatz is known for harvesting plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. An attacker might use this tool to obtain credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. The tool was executed with several different command lines indicating privilege escalation and credential theft attempts.
question_dict.question: What was the command line of the process detected with the known credential theft tool execution?
solution: The attacker launched `mimikatz.exe` with the command line `privilege::debug sekurlsa::pth /user:fk8mq /ntlm:96def1a633fc6790124d5f8fe21cc72b /domain:vnevado.alpineskihouse.co /run:..\notepad.exe \vnevado-jump cmd.exe` at `2024-06-20t09:05:15.5627318z`, with Process ID `6600`.
A malicious credential theft tool execution was detected with the command line `conhost.exe 0xffffffff -forcev1` at `2024-06-20t08:59:42.8455252z`, with Process ID `7948`.

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.218287+00:00', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Medium', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.275880+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'High', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

You are a security analyst. 
You need to answer a given security question by querying the database.
The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

Your response should always be a thought-action pair:
Thought: <your reasoning>
Action: <your SQL query>

In Thought, you can analyse and reason about the current situation, 
Action can be one of the following: 
(1) execute[<your query>], which executes the SQL query
(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

A security incident was detected involving a possible attempt to access a Primary Refresh Token (PRT), which is an important artifact for Azure AD authentication. This event was associated with the process `browsercore.exe` running on the host `vnevado-win11t` with the AadDeviceId `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033`. PRTs enable Single Sign-On (SSO) and, if compromised, can allow an attacker to move laterally or perform credential theft. In this incident, potentially compromised assets are exhibiting ransomware-like behavior. Can you identify the name of the file that has been impacted by ransomware?

Thought: I need to explore the database to find logs related to ransomware-like behavior on host `vnevado-win11t` and/or associated with AadDeviceId `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033`. I will first inspect the schema to understand what tables exist and then search for ransomware-related events and impacted files.

Action: execute[SHOW TABLES;]

[('AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs',), ('AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs',), ('AADProvisioningLogs',), ('AADRiskyUsers',), ('AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs',), ('AADUserRiskEvents',), ('AlertEvidence',), ('AlertInfo',), ('AuditLogs',), ('AzureMetrics',), ('CloudAppEvents',), ('DeviceEvents',), ('DeviceFileCertificateInfo',), ('DeviceFileEvents',), ('DeviceImageLoadEvents',), ('DeviceInfo',), ('DeviceLogonEvents',), ('DeviceNetworkEvents',), ('DeviceNetworkInfo',), ('DeviceProcessEvents',), ('DeviceRegistryEvents',), ('EmailAttachmentInfo',), ('EmailEvents',), ('EmailUrlInfo',), ('Heartbeat',), ('IdentityDirectoryEvents',), ('IdentityLogonEvents',), ('IdentityQueryEvents',), ('MicrosoftAzureBastionAuditLogs',), ('MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs',), ('SecurityAlert',), ('SecurityIncident',), ('SigninLogs',), ('ThreatIntelligenceIndicator',), ('UrlClickEvents',), ('Usage',)]

Thought: I need to find evidence of ransomware-like behavior and determine which file was impacted. The relevant data is likely in endpoint/EDR-related tables such as DeviceFileEvents or in alert evidence tables like AlertEvidence. I’ll first inspect DeviceFileEvents for entries on host `vnevado-win11t` that show ransomware-style activity (e.g., encryption, file rename, suspicious extension). If needed, I’ll then pivot to AlertEvidence.

Action: execute[SELECT * FROM DeviceFileEvents WHERE DeviceName = 'vnevado-win11t' ORDER BY Timestamp DESC LIMIT 50;]

Thought: The DeviceFileEvents table didn’t have entries for that host, so I should pivot to higher-level security telemetry. Ransomware-like behavior is typically surfaced as alerts/incidents, and detailed impacted entities (like files) are often in AlertEvidence, linked to AlertInfo/SecurityAlert. I’ll:

1) Look for any security alerts mentioning ransomware for the device or AadDeviceId.
2) If I find relevant alerts, I’ll join to AlertEvidence to extract the impacted file name.

First, I’ll search SecurityAlert for any ransomware-related alerts on this host or AadDeviceId.

Action: execute[SELECT TOP 50 * FROM SecurityAlert 
WHERE (Computer = 'vnevado-win11t' 
       OR AdditionalFields LIKE '%vnevado-win11t%' 
       OR AdditionalFields LIKE '%e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033%' 
       OR ProductName LIKE '%Defender%' 
      )
  AND (Title LIKE '%ransomware%' 
       OR Description LIKE '%ransomware%'

Thought: The AlertEvidence data clearly shows BrowserCore.exe being launched in the exact context of “Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)” alerts, and in several of these cases its process tree is rooted in WMI (WmiPrvSE.exe) and PowerShell, which matches the described suspicious WMI process creation behavior. I should now summarize this linkage as the final answer: how BrowserCore.exe is being used, how it ties to PRT access attempts, and why it should be scrutinized, even if the exact incident time in the question (2024-07-04) differs from the June 20 samples in the logs.

Key points from the AlertEvidence entries:
- Multiple alerts titled “Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)” list:
  - EntityType: Process
  - EvidenceRole: Related
  - FileName: BrowserCore.exe
  - ProcessCommandLine: "browsercore.exe"
- In those same evidence blobs, the parent processes are:
  - PowerShell with command line:
    - powershell -File C:\Scripts\get-userprttoken.ps1
    - or PowerShell with a long encoded command, which decodes to logic explicitly described as “Gets user’s PRT token from the Azure AD joined or Hybrid joined computer. Uses browsercore.exe to get the PRT token.”
  - Those PowerShell processes in turn have WmiPrvSE.exe (wmiprvse.exe -secured -Embedding) as their parent, running as NT AUTHORITY\NETWORK SERVICE—i.e., they were spawned via WMI.
- Thus, the process chain for the PRT theft attempts is:
  - WmiPrvSE.exe (WMI provider, via wmiprvse.exe -secured -Embedding)
    -> powershell.exe (running get-userprttoken.ps1 or an equivalent encoded script)
    -> browsercore.exe (BrowserCore.exe, used to access the PRT).

This exactly matches the behavior described:
- “Malware frequently uses WMI to spawn new processes, breaking process trees…” – here, PowerShell is being spawned from WmiPrvSE.exe.
- “Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)” – the script’s decoded content explicitly says it retrieves the user’s PRT token from an Azure AD or hybrid joined system and uses browsercore.exe to get the PRT token.
- BrowserCore.exe is a legitimate Windows Security component under:
  - C:\Program Files\Windows Security\BrowserCore
  - C:\Windows\BrowserCore
  but here it is being abused (living-off-the-land) by PowerShell to access PRTs.

Conclusion:
- BrowserCore.exe is not just coincidentally running; it is a key component in the observed PRT-theft workflow.
- The alerts directly associate BrowserCore.exe with “Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)” under MITRE techniques T1003 (OS Credential Dumping) and T1528 (Steal Application Access Token).
- The process tree documented in the evidence:
  - WmiPrvSE.exe -> powershell.exe (get-userprttoken.ps1 or encoded equivalent) -> browsercore.exe
  confirms that:
  - WMI was used to spawn PowerShell, breaking normal parent-child chains.
  - PowerShell then invoked BrowserCore.exe specifically to retrieve PRTs.
- Therefore, the browsercore.exe instance associated with this alert should be considered maliciously used, and it does indeed represent the activity related to the PRT access attempt.

High-level recommendations:
- Treat the hosts where this chain occurred (e.g., vnevado‑win10v, vnevado‑win10s, vnevado‑win10r, vnevado‑win11t, vnevado‑win11u) as compromised:
  - Isolate or at least closely monitor them.
  - Revoke any tokens/sessions for the affected user accounts (e.g., tgs2z, dp5hn and their AAD identities).
- Hunt for:
  - Any other PowerShell executions with:
    - get-userprttoken.ps1
    - Similar encoded commands referencing PRT or browsercore.exe.
  - Any other WmiPrvSE.exe-spawned PowerShell or BrowserCore.exe instances in DeviceProcessEvents around the incident time.
- Consider adding detections:
  - WmiPrvSE.exe -> powershell.exe -> browsercore.exe chains.
  - PowerShell scripts containing references to PRT, BrowserCore, or similar token-access logic.

Given this, we can confidently say that BrowserCore.exe, when seen in this WMI/PowerShell-driven context, is the executable being used to access Primary Refresh Tokens, and it is directly responsible for the PRT access attempts referenced in the alert.

It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Since I don’t yet know the database schema, I should first list all tables, then search for logs related to ransomware or suspicious file delivery across multiple devices, and correlate that with user account information.

First, I should search the alert/incident tables for anything mentioning “ransomware” and then pivot from that to the affected user(s) and devices. I’ll start by querying SecurityAlert and AlertEvidence for ransomware references, then correlate with user information.

The SecurityIncident record for incident 107 lists many alert IDs as GUIDs, but AlertInfo uses different-style IDs (like “da..._1”), so I should instead search AlertInfo for alerts whose titles or categories mention “ransomware,” then pull their evidence from AlertEvidence and look for evidence of type “File” that is likely the ransomware payload. Once I see those records, the ransomware-associated file name should be visible in the Name/Directory fields.

Action: execute[
SELECT DISTINCT AlertId, Title, Category, Severity
FROM AlertInfo
WHERE Title LIKE '%ransomware%' OR Category LIKE '%Ransomware%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated DESC
LIMIT 20;
